body: فتحت مصالح الأمن الإقليمي بالجديدة، بحثا قضائيا تحت إشراف النيابة العامة المختصة، للكشف عن ظروف وملابسات وفاة شخص بالمستشفى الإقليمي، وتحديد الأسباب الحقيقية التي أدت إلى وفاته، وما إذا كانت تحيط بها شبهة جنائية. وأفادت معطيات أمنية أن النيابة العامة أمرت بإيداع جثة الهالك بمستودع الأموات، قصد إخضاعها للتشريح الطبي الذي من شأنه تحديد أسباب الوفاة، في وقت باشرت فيه المصالح الأمنية الاستماع إلى أفراد من عائلته، فضلا عن تحصيل إفادات كل الأشخاص الذين يحتمل ارتباطهم بهذه القضية. وتعود تفاصيل الواقعة إلى مساء 30 أكتوبر الماضي، حين دخل الهالك في خلاف مع عناصر الحراسة الخاصة بملهى ليلي، تزامنا مع تدخل أمني باشرته عناصر الشرطة القضائية بمفوضية أزمور لتوقيف شخص مبحوث عنه بموجب قضايا تتعلق بمخالفة القانون. وتتواصل الأبحاث القضائية، تحت إشراف النيابة العامة، لتحديد طبيعة الأحداث التي سبقت وفاة المعني بالأمر، والكشف عن جميع الملابسات المحيطة بها، في انتظار ما ستسفر عنه نتائج التشريح الطبي والتحريات الجارية. المقالة التحقيق في وفاة شخص بمستشفى الجديدة fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

title: بسبب مونديال 2030.. لقجع يتخذ قرارًا مهمًا بشأن منصبه داخل الكاف
summary: قرار مفاجئ
body: قرار مفاجئ يبدو أن فوزي لقجع يستعد لإعادة ترتيب أوراقه داخل الاتحاد الإفريقي لكرة القدم، في خطوة قد تنهي إحدى أبرز مسؤولياته داخل أروقة الكرة الإفريقية، بعدما اتجه نحو تقديم استقالته من رئاسة اللجنة المالية التابعة لـ"الكاف"، مع احتفاظه بمنصبه كنائب أول لرئيس الاتحاد القاري. وذكر موقع "هسبورت" المغربي أن لقجع قرر الاستقالة من رئاسة اللجنة المالية، بسبب حجم الالتزامات التي تفرضها هذه المهمة، وما تتطلبه من تنقلات وسفريات متكررة، إلى جانب الوقت الكبير اللازم لمتابعة الملفات المختلفة المرتبطة بإدارة الشؤون المالية للاتحاد الإفريقي. وأضاف أن القرار يأتي في إطار رغبة المسؤول المغربي في إعادة ترتيب أولوياته، والتفرغ بصورة أكبر للمسؤوليات الملقاة على عاتقه داخل المغرب، سواء على الصعيد الرياضي أو الحكومي، فضلًا عن الانخراط في الملفات المتعلقة بالتحضيرات لاستضافة نهائيات كأس العالم 2030. وشدد المصدر ذاته على أن مغادرة لقجع رئاسة اللجنة المالية لا تعني انسحابه من هياكل الاتحاد الإفريقي لكرة القدم، إذ سيواصل أداء مهامه بصفته نائبًا أول لرئيس "الكاف"، محتفظًا بموقعه داخل القيادة التنفيذية للاتحاد القاري. وكان لقجع قد اكتسب خبرة كبيرة خلال فترة إشرافه على اللجنة المالية، إذ تابع عددًا من الملفات المهمة المتعلقة بالحوكمة والتوازنات المالية، فضلًا عن ترشيد النفقات والعمل على تعزيز الموارد المالية…

title: I almost died from flu. My life didn't go back to normal after.
summary: Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.
body: In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems. In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine , roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. body: A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds. The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga . Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach. title: Physicists sank a telescope 1.5 miles under the sea to put Einstein's relativity to the test
summary: A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.
body: The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible. (Image credit: Edward Berbee/Nikhef) A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks. The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA) , detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France. body: Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports. The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago. At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia. After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said. body: One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower. Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA , fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus . The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5. Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time. title: When dinosaurs are sold to the highest bidder, we all lose
summary: The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history, say Kristi Curry Rogers and Lindsay Zanno.
body: Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place. On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024. Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors. body: Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints. The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One , found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis , which is known to increase the risk of heart failure. This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation. But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats ( 80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth. title: Traces of ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, new study claims

body: Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims. However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells. In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS , the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin. The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali . While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils , this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones. "Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. title: Blue whales have gone missing off the Galápagos. Scientists think El Niño could be why.
summary: Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.
body: For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale. The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year. This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing. Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant. summary: How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.
body: The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today. Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang , the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light. Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe." "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark." The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes , an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin. The findings , presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations. In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it. More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me." body: Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf. "As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder , a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings . However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance , in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. body: Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors. In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models. RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development. This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input. title: Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
summary: Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.
body: Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice. The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans ( Homo sapiens ) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal. "Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger , a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement .
